utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted and Sebastiaan van Hooydonk for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Ms. Deirdre Montgomery, and Ms. Tatjana Savic, appearing for Stanisic Defence this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Aleksandar Aleksic, and Miroslav Cuskic, appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there's nothing to delay us, could we move immediately to have the usher escort the witness back to the stand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Sajinovic, good afternoon to you. As we begin another day of testimony, I remind you you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Sajinovic, did you and the other -- or the former member of the Milos group who is the -- responsible for communications, did the two of you have a conversation with Vojin Bera in June or July of 2010 about the flow of intelligence information from Mr. Radulovic up the internal chain of command of the RS MUP in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I cannot remember talking with him about the information that you mentioned. I don't think I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's start with, did you and the other member of the Milos group that I mentioned, did you have a conversation with Mr. Bera in around June/July of 2010?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I honestly don't remember when was the last time I saw Mr. Bera. I'm not sure that I ever talked to him in the last year or two. I don't know. Now, as for the other member of the team, I see him on a daily basis. He is a friend of mine, and he is my children's godfather.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll try this one more time. You are, of course, aware that Mr. Radulovic testified before this Tribunal last year. After his testimony, did you have a conversation with Mr. Bera concerning that, issues raised during that testimony?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I'm going to repeat what I already said twice, and I can tell you that I cannot remember. Frankly speaking, I don't remember seeing Mr. Bera. It might have happened that I came across him by accident, but what you are asking me specifically about, and the conversation with him, this is something that I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Then I'll have to move on. Sir, you've testified that the Milos group was in Doboj in the mid-May time-period. Does that mean that you arrived after the takeover of Doboj town by the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And for how long did you remain in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly at this moment for how long we stayed in Doboj. We were there, I don't know, a couple of days. Seven, ten, days. I really cannot remember. It's been a long time ago. But I do know that it was after the takeover that you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have on the screen 1D303, tab 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. We have in front of us a 12 May 1992 Milos report, numbered 125/92. And if we can read -- it begins about halfway through: "There is panic in Doboj and the town can hardly be expected to keep its current status because an attack on it is being prepared from the direction of Gracanica, Maglaj, Bosanski Brod and Tesanj. Since we are reporting from Doboj please forward this urgently to the chief of the Banja Luka CSB and request suggestions regarding our further status in this area." Mr. Sajinovic, you will agree that this is an example of Mr. Radulovic, again, using Belgrade to communicate with Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I recognise the document that I can see on the monitor as being one of the documents produced by the Milos group. Now, one can discern from the text where we were and that Mr. Radulovic was asking some suggestions from Belgrade, just as you read it. Everything is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, he's asking, not suggesting. He is asking Belgrade to forward urgently to Mr. Zupljanin this message and request suggestions regarding further status. So he is asking Belgrade to do something on his behalf; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is asking Belgrade to relay the message to Mr. Zupljanin, just as it says in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall what was the issue regarding your status in Doboj, that he was wanting clarification from Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot remember, Mr. Prosecutor. It was a long time ago. And this note is not helpful. I don't know what they were specifically referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 20004. It's tab 12. What we have in front of us is a 13 May 1992 Milos report, 132/92. Can you confirm this is one of the -- your team's reports?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Yes, it's one of our reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, this report was sent the very next day from the previous report we just looked at. And it states that according to the latest reports, there is no imminent danger of a direct attack on Doboj by Croatian armed forces and Muslim armed forces although the security situation is still difficult. So will you agree that as it turned out, there was no attack planned on Doboj at that time after all? In other words, what was stated in the prior report of an attack that was about to happen, in fact, turned out to be incorrect.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I cannot agree. You are putting me in a certain context as if I were on the side of Croats or the Muslims and that I knew what was their plan. I really didn't know what their plans were, and, therefore, I cannot agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's not what I'm suggesting. Mr. Radulovic here in this report is indicating that the intelligence, now, was that no attack was imminent, as of the very next day, there was no attack that was imminent; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the fighting around Doboj happened 2 or 3 kilometres from Doboj, if I remember correctly. That means that every minute virtually there was a possibility for the Serbian defence line to be broken through and to have enemy forces entering the town. If that's what you're asking me about. Now, as for the report that we saw on the screens a moment ago, it says clear that according to the latest information, which means at the moment when the report was being written, there was no imminent danger of attack. They even say the exact hour when this report was produced which was not the common practice with our reports. That means that on the 12th of May -- on 13th of May at 1200 hours, there was no danger. Maybe the situation changed at 1300 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. Let's take a look at 65 ter 20122. This is tab 11. So this is a 12 May 1992 Milos report numbered 126/92. I'm not showing you them in chronological order because this one is actually the date of the first Doboj document I showed you, and it reports: "... an artillery attack on the Muslim village of Grapska, Doboj municipality, caused very many civilian casualties, including children." How far is Grapska from Doboj?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you haven't shown me the reports in the chronological order, the one was from 13 and now one is from the 12th. Now, as for the village of Grapska, I'm not sure. It's not far from Doboj, but I can't tell you how many kilometres. I wouldn't like to speculate. Anyway, it's not far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And being in Doboj, do you recall how the Muslim citizens who remained in Doboj town reacted to the news of this attack on a nearby village? How did they react?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As much as I try, I really cannot remember. I don't think that everybody had all the information at the time. You're asking me about the Muslims' reaction. I was in contact with all the citizens of Doboj on a daily basis, regardless of their ethnicity, so I don't know, although I've read this note, I really don't remember this incident of shelling. I'm not familiar with that. So, at this point in time, I really cannot remember. Therefore, it would be very difficult for me to describe to you how they felt. The situation was bad. There was no electricity. I don't know how relevant the information was that was produced in the media. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But can you confirm this one of the Milos team reports?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Aleksic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to my learned friend Mr. Olmsted. Just for the clarity of the transcript, page 6, line 16, it is written "I was in contact." Although I think that the witness said otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll clarify that matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you clarify, does -- just to make sure the transcript is correct. It's not because we're accusing of you anything. But can you confirm for us that were not, in fact, in contact with all the citizens in Doboj town at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. And that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you confirm this document we have in front of us, that this is one of the Milos team's reports. It's the format and it has the handwriting that we expect.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Concerning the format, the signature, and the handwriting, I can recognise this document as the document of the Milos group. Now, as far as the contents are concerned, I already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May you please take off your headphones for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, we would like to tender these two exhibits into evidence as 65 ter 20004 and 20122.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits P2401 and 2402, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned during your examination-in-chief that there were about five SDB Banja Luka officers present in Doboj during this period of May investigating and taking statements from people "involved in fighting against the Serbian people." I take it by that you meant you were questioning -- or they were questioning non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, it is not true that this is what I said. I said that, at the time, there was a group made up of five or six members of the State Security Service in Doboj, and if I remember correctly, in a private session, I even gave you three names of members of that group. Now you're talking about two members. That's as far as this is concerned. Now, concerning their role and their activities while they were transferred from Banja Luka to Doboj, I know that they conducted interviews with people who were of interest for the service. And I think that this is what I said and I'm repeating it today. I allow for the possibility, though, that quite a few people of those were non-Serbs, but if there were any Serbs who were of interest for the security service, they would have been interviewed as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But just to make sure I'm absolutely clear on this: These state security inspectors, they were Banja Luka -- Banja Luka state security inspectors who were transferred temporarily to Doboj to assist with interrogations.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's been translated to me that they were from Banja Luka and that they were transferred temporarily to Banja Luka. Okay. Yes, that's correct, if that's what you said. They were the SDB members of Banja Luka, and they were, I might say, seconded to do their duties temporarily in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And for how long were they engaging in these activities in Doboj; if you recall?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly the duration of the period, but I know that they stayed behind in Doboj after we'd left. I know that one of those inspectors remained permanently in Doboj; that is to say, he got a permanent job there and continued living and working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who -- if you know, who temporarily reassigned them to Doboj?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know that. I can only assume how the procedure should have been implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It would have required Mr. Kesic's authorisation at the very least; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That's what I meant when I said that I suppose how it should have been. And I wouldn't say at least. I think that Mr. Kesic's approval or authorisations would suffice, and also Mr. Zivkovic's request was required, who was, at the time, the chief of the state security in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us why it was necessary for the CSB Banja Luka to assist Doboj in conducting these interrogations?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like in case of the previous question that you asked me in view of my position within the hierarchy, I can tell you that I really don't know. I really want to be 100 percent sincere. I can tell you what my opinion is, if you are interested to hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's not necessary. Do you know -- do you know if there were a significant, a large number of non-Serbs who had been arrested and detained during this time-period? Were you aware of that? And, of course, I'm speaking of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you that. Whatever I would say, it would amount to speculation. During our stay there, I never saw any kind of facility or collection centre where those people were detained. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, you were aware there was a Doboj prison right behind the police building, or right -- right near it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It was quite close to the police station, the Doboj prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And were you aware that non-Serbs were being detained there during this time-period, awaiting their interrogations?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that, but it makes complete sense to me to detain people there, whatever their nationality is, who are to be interrogated and processed. That was the case before the war, and this prison serves the same purpose even nowadays. The only thing I know about the prison, now that you mention it, is something that I heard from Radulovic; that is, that 80 to 90 per cent of the prison employees were non-Serbs. I think that we wrote some kind of report in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That was a report that you saw during proofing last week.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that report, I don't know if it was in Banja Luka or in The Hague, but I remember it, and I remember the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: These state security inspectors from Banja Luka, where did they conduct their interrogations? Was it at the CSB building?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was in the CSB building and at the police station in Doboj; but that's the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And do you recall who brought these non-Serbs in for their interrogation by -- by the state security? Were they escorted in by police officers?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, the policemen from that police station in Doboj brought them in. But, as I've said already, I was perhaps only once or twice outside that building and inside that building during all the time we were in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now while these state security Banja Luka officials were in Doboj, to whom were they submitting the reports of their activities?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't be sure because I was not there when they submitted those reports, but it would seem logical that they submitted them to the chief of the state security in Doboj, because they came from that area where they worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. But their supervisors were in Banja Luka. So would they have to report on their daily activities back to Banja Luka so that -- that the -- their superiors in Banja Luka were aware of the activities they were engaged in?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you know that for a fact, then you must be right. I don't know. It's not logical to me that they would report to their superiors in Banja Luka while a war was going on because the practice was when somebody is seconded to a different unit, the chief in that area becomes in charge of them. The same worked in the army. When a member of a military unit from Banja Luka was reassigned to a different unit in a different area, the commander in that area became their superior. It's possible, of course, these state security officers sometimes reported to Banja Luka, back to Banja Luka, but I don't think that they would make daily reports to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What you just told us reassigning from one region to another -- oh, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really apologise to my learned friend Mr. Olmsted, but it was not my intention to interrupt. But page 11, last line, the witness said something quite different from what was recorded. This thing about a military unit, I don't think the witness said that. Could Mr. Olmsted perhaps clarify with the witness what he actually said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, yes, I can do that. I have been asked to clarify something you just said for the record. You were talking about reassignment from one area to another. Can repeat what you told us about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you put the question again specifically, maybe it would be easier to answer. But if you meant the reporting by the group of operatives who were in Doboj, who had been reassigned from Banja Luka to Doboj, I said it would seem to me that they would be reporting to the state security chief, that is, the -- the line of work to which they belonged but in that area, not the area from which they were reassigned. And I used one example; namely, my colleagues, policemen, when they were assigned to the front line, would fall under the command of the military commander in whose area of responsibility they were. So during their stint on the front line, they were no longer answerable to the chief of police station. They were answerable to the commander in that area where they were seconded. In this case, that would be the chief of the centre for national security or state security, as you wish, in Doboj. If that's what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So you're drawing a parallel between an instance of being resubordinated from the police to the military, to being temporarily sent to another region to assist with interrogations. Is that what you're trying to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. It's not an objection. But I have an observation. The word used by the witness "otkomanda" was interpreted three times in different ways. Once it was "transferred." The second time, "reassigned." And the third time as "seconded." And I think that might be a problem. I don't know definitively what the proper translation is for the word he is using. And I think that it might be the problem in the communication between the witness and Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You don't know under what arrangements these state security persons were sent from Banja Luka to Doboj, do you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You already asked a similar question, and I told you my opinion, and I told you what I know. I know they worked in Doboj at the State Security Service, and they conducted interviews on the premises of the State Security Service; that is to say, the state security sector in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you're not referring to any particular regulations as to what happens when a police officer assists in another region with regard to their chain of command. You can't direct us to any particular regulation or law with regard to that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is not crystal-clear to me, to be honest, but I was trying to be frank and to explain. You -- you said a moment ago I was trying to make some comparisons and parallels, which I'm not trying to do. I'm just trying to explain how things worked at the time, in the area where I worked, where I lived, where I spent time, because you said it makes sense for colleagues who were in Doboj to report back to their superiors in Banja Luka. The colleagues who were seconded from Banja Luka to Doboj. I said it doesn't makes sense to me, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. I'm going move on. You testified that members of the Banja Luka Special Police Detachment provided security for these state security officers from Banja Luka while they were in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say something like that in response to a question either from you or somebody from the Defence. At that time, there was several members of the police unit -- the special police unit from Banja Luka who were the security detail for the inspectors of the State Security Service who were working in Doboj at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, if you know, who within the CSB Banja Luka would have assigned those special police officers that duty?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand. Who from the CSB Banja Luka would be assigned to that duty? The duty to provide security to these colleagues? That would be the members of the special police unit. Perhaps this is a confusion due to misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me try the question one more time. If you know, only if you know, can you tell us who within the CSB Banja Luka leadership would have assigned those special police -- special police officers to this duty to guard or protect the state security officials in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the question now. The answer, however, is: I don't know. Because you said in your question "only if you know." I don't know. I can only tell you what I can guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And -- yes, exactly. And if I don't put that, "if you know" before every question just assume it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can we have document ID FI 20-0185-ET on the screen, please. This is tab 53. And, Your Honours, this is, in essence, Exhibit 2D89, but it's the corrected translation that we are still waiting for the final procedural resolution of it. But as we have to show it to witnesses, I want to use it with this witness. And there's also a B/C/S version link to it as well. And I have been just told by my Case Manager that we need to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The B/C/S version is FI 20-0185-1. Now that we have both on the screen can we zoom into the names on the list, the 17 or 18 or 15 names there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Sajinovic, I know that this list is a bit hard to read. But can you tell us if you recognise any of these individuals as the special police detachment members who were assigned to protect the Banja Luka state security officers while they were in Doboj? And I understand that it was only a few that were assigned to that particular task, but maybe you could find those three or four individuals among these 15.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, out of these 15 names, I -- I just don't see 15. If maybe we zoom in a little more. This is better. Well, out of these 15 persons listed here, if I can correctly make out the names and surnames, I recognise two or three as members of the special police unit, special detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. But my question to you is: Do you recognise the names of the individuals who were in Doboj providing protection to the state security inspectors in May of 1992? Do you see their names on this list?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, of course I didn't know the names of all those people, but I can -- I can say that I've seen two or three of these in Doboj. At least out of those whose names I can make out. People whom I know personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you give us -- there's a number next to each name. Can you give us the number, the entry number, of the people you recognise?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for instance, number 1. Number 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Any others?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that number 2 was a member of the special police detachment, but I don't remember seeing him in Doboj. And as for the rest, I can't make out three, four, five of these names. And as far as the others are concerned, I can't recognise their names as those of members of the special police unit from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine. I understand it's difficult to read. But at least number 1 and number 13, those Banja Luka special detachment -- special police detachment members were in Doboj providing protection in May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now if we can just scroll up and over to the right hand corner I want to zoom in on the handwriting on the upper right-hand corner. Zoom in as much as you can, because it is also a little bit difficult to read. Now we see in the upper right-hand corner, we see the name Slavica Komljenovic, C-o-m-l-y-e-n-o-v-i-c [sic]. She's up -- her name is handwritten up there at the top. Who was she in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this also indicates her job title. And I do know that the lady with this name was a technical secretary at the CSB Banja Luka, and I remember her name, Slava, Slavica. And her job title reminded me of her.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you read out for us her job title? Because it is not presented well in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to read the whole heading?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That would be great. That would be terrific.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the presence of the tek. Secretary of the CSB Banja Luka, Slavica," and I don't really see how the last name read but it begins with a K an ends in ovic. "... received column and somebody's signature."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you knew the technical secretary at the CSB was Slavica Komljenovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: I know there was a Slavica at the CSB who was the technical secretary and I'm not sure I ever knew her surname. But if that's written here, I have no reason to doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And do you recognise the signature underneath it, whose signature that belongs to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know where we stand on this -- on this translation, but I guess we just leave it be for now. We have it in the record under its document ID number if we need to cross-reference it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, because I understand that the problems haven't been fully resolved yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now you also testified there were other members of the Banja Luka Special Police Detachment in the Doboj region, and you would see them as you came and went from the town.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have P1337, tab 13, on the screen. And let's take a look at the second page briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, you can see this is a 17 May 1992 Milos report, numbered 133/92. I think you were shown this during your 2004 interview with Investigator Nicolas Sebire. And at the time, you told him that this -- you didn't write this one, in particular?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In response to your question, I can identify this as a Milos group report under that date. But I really can't remember what your colleague showed me in 2004. But it's not a problem. You can ask me whatever you want. Now, if the question was whether I wrote this report ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That was the question. If we can turn back to the first page. And if you need to take a look at it to refresh your memory, just --

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be good. Do I need to read the whole report?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No. Just enough to -- to tell us whether it's correct that you did not type this one.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I do want to draw your attention to the final sentences of the first paragraph which read: "Apart from visible injuries suffered by the arrested persons there was appropriation of private property by those who were carrying out the searches. Such behaviour met with the indignation and condemnation of all honest citizens, and especially the mobilised Serbian Territorial Defence members, who threatened to use arms against the special forces from" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please be asked to tell the interpreters the reference in the B/C/S text.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In the B/C/S text, it's the first paragraph and it's -- I'm reading the last two sentences.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: "Such behaviour met with the indignation and condemnation of all honest citizens, and especially the mobilised Serbian Territorial Defence members, who threatened to use arms against the special forces from Banja Luka and the special forces organised by a man called Bozovic." Mr. Sajinovic, do you recall during this time-period Mr. Radulovic telling you about the criminal behaviour of members of the special police forces from Banja Luka while they were in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, from that period, I recall hearing, not only from Radulovic but from many other persons as well, that some kind of illegal activities, if I may put it that way, were being carried out by groups and individuals in the area of Doboj whilst we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But I am referring particularly to the members or certain members - not all members, but certain members - of the special police detachment from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke about this topic specifically with Radulovic as well. The information that we had at the time was that there were lots of stories going around about the deeds committed by members of the special unit from Banja Luka. According to what we knew, the majority of these activities were, in fact, committed by local criminals organised in groups, as well as some individuals from Doboj and its surroundings. I spoke about that yesterday. What is interesting to note here is concerning this report that we're looking at and the sentence that you just read, it says that they even threatened to put up armed resistance, in inverted commas, "to the specials of Banja Luka." When you put inverted commas in the Serbian language, that indicates not exactly what is quoted. Therefore, this leads me to believe that there were such rumours but that they were not founded. This is the only thing that I can conclude from this document and from the talks I had with Radulovic at the time regarding those illegal activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. But you didn't -- you didn't gather this intelligence. This was Mr. Radulovic. So he is the person who knew exactly what he was reporting here, obviously.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. As far as this is concerned, it's correct, and as far as I can recall the conversation that I had with Radulovic about this topic, and I heard it from him personally that everything that happened in the area of Doboj was attributed to outsiders. In this instance, those outsiders were members of the special police detachment from Banja Luka and members of special unit volunteers from Serbia led by Radojica Bozovic. If I remember correctly, I spoke about this extensively yesterday. And just briefly, not only in the Doboj area, it was typical that if anyone tried to commit a crime, and happens even today, they leave some trail in order to point or set up somebody else as a perpetrator. At the time, Bozovic's Red Berets were in Doboj, would wear hats that were worn by Mr. Talic's specials or the hats by -- worn by people from Banja Luka. So every person, every peasant in every village was able to see that although they were virtually illiterate, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before you move on, Mr. Olmsted, I would just wish to point out to you that you have an hour remaining, a half of the first session and then when we come back, you have a half-hour remaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified that you saw CSB chief Andrija Bjelosevic in Doboj one or twice. Can you tell us on what date, what occasions you saw him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't remember mentioning Mr. Andrija Bjelosevic today. You say "you just said." That's what I said maybe yesterday or the day before yesterday but not today. I told you that I saw him once or twice. I cannot remember. But that was during the period when we were in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us on what occasions you saw him? Do you recall the occasions? Did you see him at the CSB?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think either outside or inside the building, and once I just bumped into him in the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You stated that Mr. Radulovic told you where Mr. Bjelosevic was and that he was always at the Duge Njive area. Did Mr. Radulovic tell you how he knew all this information?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You put it right. I remember that he was in the area of Duge Njive. I remember asking this question because Bjelosevic was the chief of the CSB Doboj at the time, and I asked Radulovic how come we don't see him more often. And I'm trying to remember the exact name, but I think it was a staff or -- or whatever of the Doboj operations group, which was stationed in Duge Njive. As I understood at the time, apparently his activity there was to co-ordinate the defence of Doboj with the military commanders. I don't know. This is just guess-work. Anyway, that would be it, and I wouldn't like to speculate any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And while he was away, were the Doboj police reporting to his deputy?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I really didn't know, given my position, what the hierarchy in Banja Luka was. Now in you're asking me about the police, and I suppose you are referring to the uniformed police, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm referring to the CSB police, yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Banja Luka CSB, and the organisation of any CSB was similar, didn't have any police. Maybe they had some kind of dozen police officers, but not exactly police officers. Those were inspectors. So their duty was to carry out inspections of police stations. Anyway, the police was in Banja Luka but I say the same organisation was in place in Doboj, and people were organised within various police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to move now to Prijedor. If we can have P --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really apologise to my learned friend. I don't intend to interrupt him. 23, 22, lines, the witness said, "I say the same organisation was in place in Doboj." The witness said: In the public security station in Doboj. And then he added that they were organised within various police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I guess we're going to have to ask you the question again just to clarify the record because I didn't understand that interpretation. Can you repeat --

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you just repeat what you said with regard -- I assume what you're saying is that CSB Doboj was organised the same way as CSB Banja Luka, as far as the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. Let's discuss Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have P1376 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry. If we are going to clarify this, the answer of the witness, we must clarify it in its totality. And, therefore, either -- either we clarify it or Mr. Olmsted should pose the same question again, the question which he posed. Because right now in the transcript, we are getting -- we have a recording of what -- of -- I mean, adequate recording as to the answer of the witness. Thank you. I'm sorry I interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. Let me see -- I guess we're going to have to go back, and I'm going to have to go back to my prior question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: My question -- my question that really originated this was while Mr. Bjelosevic was away from the CSB, who was in charge -- who was this charge of the CSB, and you were giving us a kind of explanation of how essentially it was the same way. Can you repeat your answer again in general? Because I think, at this stage, I think we need to ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer was that I didn't know who ran the CSB, although I think that wasn't your question, but, never mind. I said that I didn't know who was at the head of the CSB whilst Mr. Bjelosevic was away. If I'm not wrong, you asked me to whom the police was reporting, and I asked you, are you referring to the uniformed police, and you said, yes, that's what you were referring to, and you were referring to the CSB police in particular. And then I said that, as far as I know, I drew a parallel between the CSB Banja Luka and the CSB Doboj because they were organised in an identical way and that applied to every CSB covered by the area of the MUP of Republika Srpska. And I said that as far as I knew, the CSB did not have police force. There were perhaps a dozen or so uniformed police officers, but they were not actual police officers who were on the beat, so to say, but, were, rather, sitting in offices and were doing the job of police inspectors and each one of them had their own area of police stations that they inspected. The police officers were within public security stations and were organised within police stations in the area covered by a specific CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Is Defence counsel satisfied? Thank you. Let's move on to Prijedor. May I have P1376, tab 15 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a 28 May 1992 Milos report numbered 162/92. Now, according to this report, you were aware at the end of May 1992 that, as it states here, a huge number of civilians from Prijedor, men, women, children, and elderly, were arrested or surrendered; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the Milos reports, and it says what you just quoted. Yes, that's one of the Milos reports; or, rather, one of Mr. Radulovic's reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, these civilians from Prijedor, they included the non-Serb population from the villages in the Hambarine and Kozarac areas; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think one can say that that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where were these persons held? What were the primary locations that they were held in?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know the situation in that period, nobody asked me anything about this over the past two days. In addition to the reception centres that I mentioned before, there was one also in the place which is, I think, called Trnopolje. According to the information that I had at the time, this is where the civilians were housed. They were put up in this reception centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Are you saying that none of them were housed at Omarska or Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the civilians, the women, the children, that we were just talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, this talks about men, women, children, and elderly. Are you saying all those persons were in Trnopolje or were they also at Omarska and Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have allow for a fact, Mr. Prosecutor, that I couldn't have known where everybody was put up. We had information that there was civilians housed in Trnopolje. Able-bodied men, conscripts, people who were captured during combat operations were accommodated in Keraterm and Omarska, as you mentioned, and I spoke about this yesterday and before yesterday; that is to say, that the information that we had at the time was that at those reception centres interviews being conducted with those people in order to carry out screening for those for whom it was established that were not responsible for being involved in armed rebellion were eventually released from Omarska and Keraterm. Now as for women, children, and elderly, I really cannot tell you that I saw them at any of those locations visited by Mr. Radulovic and myself. If need be, I can repeat that we spent a short time at Keraterm. The detainees there were in the lower part of the building, in a big hall, and we were in the administration building above. We were not at all allowed access. Now, judging by the look on your face, you want me to stop, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, yes --

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, it is difficult. I apologise. It is difficult for me to talk about the year 1992 whilst are you smiling all the time. This is really awkward for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Please, don't read anything into my expressions. I do, however, want you to try to keep to the question. You have given us a lot of information that wasn't contained within my very simple question which is that some of these civilians were actually held at Omarska and Keraterm, and I can get from your answer that the answer is yes. And that's all I'm trying to get at. But don't read anything into my expression beyond that.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is no. And please forgive me if I avert my eyes from you. You are really breaking my concentration and I really don't like the expression on your face.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified that you had intelligence information that non-Serbs in Kozarac were organising into military units and that they had an intention to take over militarily in the area. That was on -- during your examination-in-chief; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you clarify for us, by area did you mean the Prijedor municipality or were you only referring to the Kozarac area?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You would agree that if that was, indeed, the non-Serbs' intention, they were extremely outnumbered by the Serb forces at the time, including the VRS, the TO, the police, and the paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that. That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall that the 43rd Motorised Brigade was in Prijedor during this time-period?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. I wasn't very familiar with the military organisation. Since I am expected to give brief answers, I might just not mention that there was no, the Army of Republika Srpska at the time. According to the information that we had, these forces that we discussed in Prijedor were much better organised. As for the so-called Serbian forces and the Serbian population living in the area, laid all their hopes in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you aware that the 5th Kozara Light Infantry Brigade was in this -- if you know whether the 5th Kozara Light Infantry Brigade was in Prijedor at this time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you aware that the 6th Sana Brigade from the Sanski Most adjoining municipality was in the area, if you do know; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think the witness has expressed the view that he was unfamiliar with the presence of the military formations. So please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you aware there was a Serb Territorial Defence organised in Prijedor during this time headed by Slobodan Kuruzovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, believe me, that I didn't know. And I really don't recognise the name that you have just given me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have P1388, tab 25, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please enlarge it a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a 11 July 1992 Milos report, numbered 271/92. The last two sentences are what I'm interesting in. It says: "The killing of civilians in Doboj, Teslic, and Kozarac are not in favour of the Serbian dignity and the honour of the Serbian army. Then it goes on to ask: "Please explain to us what are the interests of the Serbs in creating in a violent manner ethnically cleansed entities and how we should position ourselves," et cetera, et cetera. Sir, the report doesn't mention it, but we could include civilians in Hambarine and Brezovo as well to this list.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't take it upon myself to include anyone, Mr. Prosecutor. This document speaks about the people who perished irrespective of their ethnicity. This is a very emotion subject. I don't want to categorise any people. As for the killing of people in Teslic, that's the only incident that I am aware of. We wrote about it. We arrested the group of the Serbs who committed the crime. We processed them. And that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, could you assist me by -- as to identifying what the question was? Because you -- you read portions of the report to the witness and then you declared the report doesn't mention [indiscernible] so-and-so. Where is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That was the question. That -- it -- could it as well include those two areas that aren't mentioned in this report, where a large number of civilians were killed during this time-period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, had you an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, Your Honours, I just noticed when Mr. Olmsted was reading from the -- from the translation of the -- of this document, that the translation is somewhat not correct. It contains "ethnically cleansed entities" and that doesn't appear in the original at all. Therefore, we would request that this document be re-sent to -- CLSS so we can have the proper translation. It might turn to be an important issue in this case, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Sajinovic, you had your hand up. Yes, you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think the witness wants some water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We are about to take the break shortly, but the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber would ask to you read out from the B/C/S that you would have, the relevant portion. And, Mr. Zecevic, if you would follow along, and we'd see what the -- what the interpreters say.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I think we're dealing with the last sentence in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Did the usher ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honours, do I need to read this? As Mr. Prosecutor says, this is the last sentence then. The last sentence reads in the Serbian version that I have: "Please explain to us what the interests of the Serbs in creating in a violent manner ethnically compact areas and how we should position ourselves with regard to the manifestations and the perpetrators of such activities."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, is your concern -- are your concerns resolved? Or do we -- we now have on the record what the witness says that the documents says in B/C/S. Should we nevertheless still send this for -- to be retranslated?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it is -- this translation is somewhat in between, I'm afraid, what the -- what the original says and what is the previous translation. Therefore, I would respectively ask that the document be sent to CLSS just -- it's a one -- it's a one -- one sentence only. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. And we'll take the adjournment and return for the -- so Mr. Olmsted can complete his cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May we have 65 ter 10191 on the screen, please. That's tab 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, this is a 7 September 1992 Milos report, numbered 372/92. Can you confirm this is one of the team's reports?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The format is consistent with the reports of the Milos group.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall typing up this one, in particular?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did this. In any case, I recognise the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm just going to read the first two sentences. It says: "According to our source, VAL, and a large number of contacts with citizens, we have the information that the security situation in the Prijedor area is still [sic] quite difficult and rather chaotic. In this area, buildings are still unnecessarily destroyed and citizens of Muslim and Croatian nationality forcibly expelled, even killed." After the events we were talking about before the break, in Kozarac and Hambarine in May and early June 1992, the situation didn't improve for the non-Serb population in Prijedor, did it? In fact, as this report indicates, they were being -- continued to it be killed and expelled, even into September 1992.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for the content of the report, it does say something like that what you've just read. But whether that happened, as I said when we discussed another report, it relates to that date and that period. You say continued to be. I don't know whether it continued to be. Whether it was continuous. But you can see the pseudonym on this report. So it was a source of Mr. Radulovic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, I choice the word continued because I was reading the second sentence I read, which was: "In this area buildings are still unnecessarily destroyed and citizens of Muslim and Croatian nationality forcibly expelled." So I read the "still" in the report, as meaning it was a continuing thing. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Later on in the report it mentions information or stories about mass graves. Were you -- did you have any information about those mass graves, or was this solely information that Mr. Radulovic had?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I did not have such information, and talking to Mr. Radulovic, I never heard that he had such information either. It says here that especially dangerous are stories about those locations of mass graves. And I agree, that such stories are dangerous, so I cannot confirm that it was correct and that some specific locations are meant. I really can't answer this. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2403, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 282 - this is tab 49 - on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm not a 100 per cent sure, but I think you had a look at this document back in 2004. It's a sector -- line of work 01. So line 01, state security sector, Banja Luka, survey of activities of the SNB sector Banja Luka based on the line of work for 01 for the period April 1992 to April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could we turn to page 2 of, I think, both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I want to look at the paragraph with the handwriting to the left of it. And in paragraph reads: "In such a situation, the operative composition of this sector's SNB is actively engaged in the investigations of ... detained persons," and then lists the municipalities: "... Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, Kljuc, Sanski Most, Mrkonjic Grad, Doboj, Bihac, Petrovac, Glamoc, Gradiska, Kotor Varos, and somewhat later, Jajce?" If we could scroll to the left there's some handwriting. Do you recognise that handwriting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Who does it belong to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vojin Bera.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And since that handwriting does not appear in the English version, can you just read what it says?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Doboj and Banja Luka." Before Doboj, I believe there is a letter, C, in Cyrillic, or similar. But I'm not sure. But what I clearly see is "Doboj and Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And were you aware that Vojin Bera was co-ordinator of the state security officers who were sent to the various detention facilities around the region in 1992 to conduct interrogations?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We've already talked about Doboj and a little bit about Prijedor. Were you aware that there's state security officials who were engaged in interrogations of non-Serb detains in Kljuc, Sanski Most, and Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for other places, or, rather, the places you've just mentioned, I knew that in those areas there was a presence of the operatives of state security, operatives who were responsible for those areas. And in peacetime, in the time of former Yugoslavia, the State Security Service and all the other state institutions had contingency plans for natural disasters, war, immediate threat of war and, of course, the State Security Service had those plans as well. Within the State Security Service, there were war time departments, and that means, towns, or, rather, municipalities covered by a particular centre of state security. There was one operative officer of State Security Service in charge of each war time department; for instance, the war time section of Kljuc, or Kotor Varos, or whatever. Now, what they did and who they investigated, I don't know. They were our colleagues working on an equal footing with us, and the object of our interest were not colleagues from the same service. You know what the object of our interest was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can we please turn to page 5 in the English and the B/C/S. And I'm interested in the bottom paragraph. It starts out -- well, before the numbered paragraphs it states: "Bearing in mind only certain ... elements in the estimation and in accordance with realistic possibilities, this department has focussed on the following things ..." And the first -- and I'm just going to summarise them. I'm not going to read them all out. But the first relates to discovering the pillars of intelligence, propaganda and activities among foreign citizens. The second, which is on page 2 of the English, is the gathering of information about activities of the UNPROFOR members? The third priority is organising of new immigration for the purpose of monitoring terrorist activity towards the RS, Serbs, and Serbian clubs abroad. The fourth is gathering of information about forces, locations, deployment, et cetera, of enemy formations. And, finally, the fifth is discovering of criminal acts against humanity committed against the Serb population in some regions. Can you tell us, just within the structure of the state security, who set these priorities?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You must believe me, Mr. Prosecutor, when I say that I could not answer your question with any certainty. I could make conjectures again, but you've made it quite clear you don't want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's correct. And thank you for just keeping it at that. With regard to this last objection -- objective, which is discovering of criminal acts against humanity committed against the Serb population in some regions, can you tell us, would this encompass crimes committed against Serbs in the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Have you to show me where that is. I can't see it. The last thing I see is: "Gathering information ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I apologise. Can we turn the page in the B/C/S version. I apologise for that. Number 5 is on the second -- on the next page, page 6. And if you look under number 5, it's what I just read and I just want to confirm that that included state security inspectors looking into such crimes committed in the ARK, the Autonomous Region of Krajina, as well as perhaps Doboj region and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this is a report by the Banja Luka sector of the state security, I conclude that this refers to the area covered by the state security sector in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour. Mr. Prosecutor, looking at this document, I've been thinking, and I remember I was shown this by your colleague in 2004, and that's fine. But I would appreciate it if you could show me this document page by page on the screen, or perhaps you have a hard copy. It is very important, and you will hear the reasons, Your Honours, why. I remember that I've said this to the investigator at the time, certain observations of mine, and I think this is very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Do you have a hard copy available that you may show the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me see if I have an unmarked copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hard copy would be even better. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: He can use this one, I think. It's a little bit marked up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But just ignore any blue pen mark on it.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a problem. I just want to see the printed version. Thank you again for enabling me to look at this document, and I'm very happy, indeed, that I have recalled this document. I'm not going to go into the contents at this time. The Prosecutor has read out certain passages that he interested in, and that's fine, I'm not going to comment on that. But one thing I noticed in 2004 is this: The first page of the document, the second page, the third page, the fourth page, the fifth page of the document, and the sixth page of the document were typed on one and the same typewriter. The font is the same, and even a layman can see it's one and the same typewriter. What's interesting is, at the bottom of the sixth page, the text does not end. Instead, there is a comma, and the text continued on page 7 in a different typewriter, using a different font, different letters, and the seventh, eighth, and ninth page were typed on a different typewriter. I expressed my doubts about the authenticity of this document in 2004, and I express them again for the reasons that I've stated. Since this is an overview or a survey of certain activities on page 6, in paragraph 6, it says, "As a result, based on the gathered information, in the form of notes," et cetera, "the service of national security was sent," and then blanks, so many, it doesn't say how many, Official Notes, so many communications, so many reports. So these are blanks. I explained to the investigator at the time in detail - I don't want to go into detail here now - but I believe that is somebody's attempt to misrepresent things by leaving blank the place for the number. I don't know what it is about, but I can't understand why at least two different typewriters were used. Thank you again. I hope I have been of assistance, and I apologise for using a few extra minutes of the Prosecutor's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No problem and thank you for your assistance. Can you remove your headphones for a minute while we resolve this issue.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, Mr. Aleksic was about to say something on your application. But before I hear from him, could I understand for what purpose you seek to tender this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, the purpose is -- is obviously the content and the -- particularly the areas I just covered that are in this report. As -- are we concerned about the authenticity or the contents, Your Honours? The relevance or the -- or the -- authenticity?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Both now, having regard to the witness's intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. The relevance is because it speaks about the activities of line 01 at the state security sector in Banja Luka for the period of -- from April 1992 through April 1993. So it does cover entirely the indictment period. And it discusses their activities, their priorities during that time-period. And I haven't read all those parts of it, but it also talks about the detention facilities in Prijedor, and et cetera. As far as the authenticity is concerned, of course, this witness is not an expert on -- on documents, he expresses opinion, of course, as to what it is. It could very well be a draft of a report that is eventually sent. He did authenticate the handwriting of Vojin Bera, who, at the time, during this period, was the head of line 01. So whatever stage in the drafting this was, at one point it was in the hands of Mr. Bera, who would have been the one who would have authorised this report. And so we say that there's enough to authenticate it for purposes of admission in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, do you have something to contribute to this discussion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. In addition to what the witness has said and what Mr. Olmsted said the witness identified, this document has nine pages, and the witness recognised two words in it that he says were written by Mr. Bera. The document does not bear a number, does not bear the name of the author. What I see this as is a draft version. You can see in item 5 that lines are left blank for some things to be written in. Also, Mr. Olmsted asked the witness if he knows that Mr. Bera was the co-ordinator. The witness answered in the negative. Then the Prosecutor asked if he was aware if operatives from the state security from Banja Luka went to work in other centres. The witness says: I don't know. So in addition to all the formal deficiencies of this document, the witness confirmed none of the major elements of this document, nothing important. That's what I wanted to say, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, what the Chamber doesn't understand is what exactly this is and what -- what its origin is. And to whom was it directed. None of that is apparent from the document itself, and the witness is unable to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the title page tells you what it is. It's a survey of activities of the SNB sector Banja Luka based on the line of work 01, for the period April 1992 to April 1993. And it has, at the top, it says it comes from the CSB Banja Luka, state security sector and it even has a date, 12 April 1993. And -- up to the right it says line of work, 01. And we've heard evidence that line 01 within the state security sector in Banja Luka was under Vojin Bera during this time-period. And this is a report on their activities. And we've heard that among their activities were sending state security inspectors to detention facilities to interrogate detainees, and that's included in this report. This gives us information as to what their priorities were during this time-period, what kind of work they were doing. This is part of the CSB Banja Luka. Now whether it is a draft or not, this witness obviously can't provide any information on that. But drafts can be admitted into evidence. We're not saying that this made it to the hands of anyone up the chain of command. It is dated 1993. So that is not necessary relevant for us, but what was relevant for us is the information that's contained within it. And we submit that the handwriting of Vojin Bera, the head of this section, on the page, and his handwritten notes on the page shows that he was reviewing this. So this must have been something he was considering and reviewing as to his line of work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you, anyhow -- oh, yeah, sorry. Mr. Witness, could you in any way support Mr. Aleksic's allegation that this could be a draft?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my answer would be yes, I can fully confirm that this was a draft, at best. When I say "at best," I was referring to what I spoke about earlier. And the indication of that are the lines on page 6 in the Serbian, item 5. So all the numbers are lacking, the number of reports, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2404, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Sajinovic, you'll be happy to hear I'm very near to the end. I just want to clarify just a couple of things that came up during your examination that I don't think are going to be controversial. If we can have P1369, tab 3, on the screen, please. And had you a chance to look at this, I believe, when Mr. Aleksic was asking you questions. I'm not going to ask you any questions about the content. What I'm interested in is if you look at the bottom, the reference number is 49/92. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you see that the date of this Milos report is 2 April 1992.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. Remember that, and let's take a look at 1D293.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tab number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It was a Defence -- it was your tab, so if you could help us out, that would be great. I didn't write down the tab. It's a Defence document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But for purposes of this, you won't need to see the hard copy. I just want you to look at the reference number on this one. Now, this one is reference number 53/92. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now this one doesn't have a date on it. But can we draw the conclusion that since its reference number is subsequent to the reference number of the previous document, that this one was written after that. In other words, the reference numbers are sequential: The first number being the number of the report, and the second number being the year.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. What you said last that first comes the number of the report and then the year. Now when you asked me whether I would be able to draw a conclusion, if I understood you correctly, whether this document preceded the previous one, according to the number, that could be the case. But I have equally seen quite a few documents of ours without any number or date on them. And when I was giving my answers the day before yesterday, I said that one of my colleagues whose handwriting I identified here used to establish this register in 1994. So I cannot say with any degree of certainty whether this document was produced earlier. Just let me tell you that I didn't read the contents. I was just focussing on the form and the format.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that's exactly what I want you to focus on. But just to clarify: The one we looked at before had the reference number 49/92 while this one has the reference number 53/92. So I was asking you whether this meant that the one in front of us came after the previous one, because it's later -- it's a higher reference number, indicating that it was further along in the reporting cycle.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave you an answer. According to the number that you quoted, it would only make sense that it came later. However, I cannot confirm that for the reasons that I gave you. There is no date, and, as I said, I've seen many reports of ours missing numbers and dates, et cetera. So, whatever you say makes sense; but also whatever I say makes sense. I am under oath, and, therefore, I cannot claim with any certainty that this document was produced after the first one. But the format is consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think you've already testified that the person who maintained these files was the third member of the Milos team, who was responsible for communications.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. What I told you is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Final clarification. If we can have 2D84 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's our tab 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And had you a chance to look at this during your examination. And I just want to draw your attention to the end of the document, the last two sentences. It says: "Please keep Becirevic in custody until our arrival so that we can conduct a detailed interview concerning these and other circumstances." Can you confirm with us, is that Dzemo Becirevic? Is that the person you are referring to there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us, you -- this is requesting that he be held in custody until you arrive. Where was he being held?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should first ask the question: Who held him; and then the location. I can only deduce something about who held him in custody, but I don't know anything about the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. Could you answer who was holding him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the language of the document, I would say that this gentleman was in custody in Serbia, which means that, according to this document, he was kept in custody by the RDB members in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And by RDB, you mean the Serbian MUP. That -- the security services within the Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say RDB, stands for State Security Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And it says hold him until we conduct a detailed interview. Do I take it that you did not go out to Serbia to conduct this interview if it, in fact, occurred?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I myself didn't go, and I don't remember whether Mr. Radulovic went. I'm not aware of that. When we discussed a similar note -- I'm sorry, no. I misspoke. So, I don't remember, and I don't know if Mr. Radulovic went.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. And maybe the note you're thinking about, let's turn to 2D86.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And perhaps my learned friend can help me with the tab number on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 12.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand which particular note you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
