utterances.text: Well, just take a look at this one. You were shown this one as well during your examination. I'm not sure if it was by Mr. Aleksic or by Mr. Cvijetic. But do you recall taking a look at this document during your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm interested in the first paragraph at the very end. It says that a statement was taken from Dzemo Becirevic at -- in September 1992 at the premises of the VIZ in Banja Luka. I understand by VIZ that's a military prison. Can you tell me, is that Mali Logor or is that some other facility in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you are right. Is this abbreviation stands for the military remand prison. As far as I know, such prison existed within the compound of the Mali Logor barracks in Banja Luka, but I really don't know whether the military had such prisons elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us how Mr. Becirevic was transferred from Serbia back to Banja Luka; if you know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I really cannot comment on this. Whether he was transferred or not, and, if so, how, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you take part in this interview of him at the Mali Logor prison? I take it by your answer you probably didn't because you're not quite sure of the name.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On behalf of what? I'm not sure. But you are right. I didn't take part in this interview. All I know is that this gentleman was interviewed on several occasions, and I think that I did take part in one or two, but not at this location that is mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: At which location did you interview him at?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the premises of the National Security Centre in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So at the CSB building.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The State Security Service was within the CSB building in Banja Luka in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could we have P1384 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I have a problem with this document, and perhaps -- perhaps it's only a translation issue. It is Mr. Radulovic sending a message to Chief Zupljanin, who, you told us, was in Belgrade. And it's about replenishment and reinforcing the reserve force with "one company of 80 well-trained and well-equipped soldiers whose status is unclear in the moment because they do not belong either to the Serbian army or to the reserve police force. Their engagement in the reserve police would also be good for preventative reasons, since individuals from this company or the entire company have got out of control and become a paramilitary formation." Now, I don't know -- I'm not asking about what you know about this. I'm asking you what it is in the B/C/S text. What company is the B/C/S text talking about? A police company? A police unit that became a paramilitary formation, or a military unit that became a military formation? What does the B/C/S text of this document tell us?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, concerning the text of this document, you are absolutely right. If I hadn't been familiar with what was happening in that area, I wouldn't have been able to understand what is written here and what you're asking me about. The unit mentioned here was a military unit, which was part of the Teslic Brigade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's your knowledge, right? That's not in the text. That's your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my knowledge. But, as you, yourself, said, if you allow me, the text says that they should be attached or become members of the reserve police. This excludes the possibility that this was a unit that was already part of the police -- police force. Next thing, it says that it is possible that they would get out of control and become a paramilitary formation. As I read this text, they haven't become a paramilitary formation yet. If you had a commander, you had a company of men who were armed, I understand this text to mean that this was a military unit. And the knowledge that I have about this period was that Mr. Josic [phoen], the commander of this company, was an active-duty serviceman in the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Sajinovic, could I just follow up on the question put by Judge Delvoie. And ask you: What was the result? Was that unit eventually resubordinated or transferred to the police?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this unit remained as part of the Teslic Brigade. In other words, it maintained the status of a military unit. The commander of this unit, as far as I know, left the area of Republika Srpska after a certain period of time and went to work in the Army of Serbia, or Yugoslavia, or whatever it was called at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: One other question, as far as I'm concerned. It's about the -- the topic of training people in police training centres in Croatia, before the war. You remember we talked about that? Men were sent by the SDA to police training centre in Croatia, while there was a centre in the republic itself; right? That was the topic. My question is: They were sent by the SDA. Who paid those men while under training? Were they paid with public funds?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know anything about that. Whatever I tell you would be in the domain of speculation. So at the time when we acquired this knowledge -- I'm sorry. For us, this aspect of what were the sources of payment was not of interest to us. We were just interested in the fact that those people were being trained and prepared for war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And your answer to a question in that -- in that regard was that this fact would be a violation of the current legislation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and of Yugoslavia. It would be an illegal activity. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, by the very fact that these men hadn't undergone certain security vetting procedures as prescribed by the law when people were recruited for police force and the fact that they were being sent to another state and not to regular police centres, as far as we know, and you, yourself, noticed this, there was regular police school in Bosnia-Herzegovina who trained policemen, and this evidently constituted the breach of the law and an illegal activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: My question still remains: What -- what is there that -- and I agree, it's a rather theoretical question. But what is there that prevents a private organisation, like a political party or whoever, to send people for -- for certain trainings; it be police training, it be security training, it be whatever. Is there any law against that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as I know, a law like that existed and still exists, because not a single political party or any other organisation except organisations responsible for carrying out certain activities such as security agencies and the police force were prohibited by law from creating their own armies and sending people to that kind of training. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sajinovic. I have one question to you that partly falls in line with the question just put to you by Judge Delvoie. If I could ask the Registrar to pull up for us on the screen, Exhibit P2503. That will show to be the Milos report from September 1992. And it raises an issue about members of the Serbian armed forces or units that were acting without the consent of the Supreme Command of the Serbian army. You will see that -- ah, there it is on the screen. And if you'd just take time to run through it.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Yes, a moment ago I was answering the Prosecutor's questions on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. My question, Mr. Sajinovic, is about the reference to the members of the Serbian armed units that were apparently active in the area around Prijedor. And what Mr. Radulovic writes here in his report is that there were allegations that the -- these members of the Serbian armed units were acting and undertaking measures without the consent of the Supreme Command of the Serbian army. Now my question is, if you can explain to us what the relations were between the Serbian army and the VRS? Because if my recollection serves me correct, I think that the VRS was established sometime in May 1992, and this dispatch is from September; That is to say, that long after the VRS was established in May, you have Serbian forces that were active in Bosnia. Are you able to explain to us what the -- what the -- what the relations were between these two armies, or were the Serbian armed forces under the VRS control or were they under, still, the Supreme Command of the Serbian army in Belgrade's authority; do you know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will very gladly answer your questions, or, rather, I would, but I'm not very qualified to talk about the relationship between one army and the other. I'm not very well informed about that. But concerning the document on the screen, it reads at one point "without the consent of the Supreme Command of the Serbian army." I think you misread this as implying that members of the Army of Serbia were present in this area. I, however, read this document, and I'm sure about this, as a reference by Mr. Radulovic to members of the army of the Serbian army in Bosnia and Herzegovina, or the Serbian units in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You certainly did, because the way that I would read the English translation of this document would suggest that the soldiers of which this dispatch makes reference to were Serbian armed units under the command of the Serbian army. It doesn't say that it was under the Supreme Command of the Bosnian Serbian army. Maybe can you read out that sentence for us and we can check for an immediate interpretation. Please? Read it out from the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I'll read it aloud. But as I've said, knowing the situation at the time in that area, and working with Radulovic, and having seen this document, I understand that it means members of the Serbian Army of Republika Srpska. And I'm beginning to read now: "In this area, buildings are still being unnecessarily destroyed and citizens of Muslim and Croatian nationality are forcibly expelled, even killed. All this has brought a lot of fear and anxiety even into the Serbian homes in this area and the feeling is increasing that members of the Serbian armed units are acting and undertaking measures without the consent of the Supreme Command of the Serb army. The political structures within the Serbian republic or the Serb republic and the general interests of the Serbian people." Should I read on

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, thank you very much for this. So it is only when we apply your interpretation to this document that we can fully understand that what Mr. Radulovic was making reference to was indeed the VRS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow me just one more thing, very briefly. Speaking of the same document. When I read a moment ago, I didn't want to interrupt, not to confuse the interpreters, but you see it says, "In this area, all this has brought a lot of fear even into the Serbian homes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. There seems to be a technical problem with the transcript so if you could just pause for a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience. I think we're back with the system running. Could you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gladly. Your Honour, I understood this passage you mentioned very well. I understood this reference to the Serbian army, and I also understood that you -- sorry, the document disappeared from the screen again. I understood that you read it as members of the Army of the Republic of Serbia. But I'm pointing out that the same passage says at one point "all this has brought a lot of fear and anxiety even into the Serbian homes." And in that case, that -- in your understanding, that would mean the homes of the nationals of Serbia in this area, which is definitely not true. This means that Serbian homes in Republika Srpska and the Serbian Army of Republika Srpska. That's all. I hope I have made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You have indeed. Thank you very much. I have no further questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Sajinovic, that brings your -- sorry. That brings your testimony to an end. Thankfully a few days early than we had anticipated when you started on Monday. So you are now released. We thank you for your assistance and we wish you a safe journey back to your home. So the usher would escort you. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. To conclude, I would like to thank the Trial Chamber, the Office of the Prosecutor, and the Defence teams. I want to say that I've done my best to contribute to the proving of the truth, and I hope I succeeded. And in the future, whenever you deem necessary, I am prepared to come again and tell you whatever I can. Thank you again. I wish you success in your work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Following on our indication yesterday about the possibility of three days being available next week, we await reports on the success of Mr. Krgovic's attempts to fill this gap. In the absence of that, at the rising of the Court today, we will reconvene in this courtroom on Tuesday, the 8th of November. So parties should keep alert to watching the e-mail traffic to see whether we will be coming in, in advance of that, to take advance of the three days next week. Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just an administrative matter. On the first day of this witness's testimony, Monday, he was shown a document, P1370.1 in private session, and at the end of that, the Prosecution moved to have that portion of the transcript in open session, but I did not provide the transcript references and that is needed by the Registry. It is T.25156, line 19, to T.25160, line 22. If that could be made in open session because the document -- the portions of the document that were redacted were not raised during the witness's testimony and therefore there's no reason for that to be in closed -- private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So ordered.
